If her husband suggested they sit together and watch a movie, or take a quiet evening on the porch, she often pulled away from the possibility of ease. To soften even briefly felt unsafe and undeserved.

These changes accumulated in her marriage and in the person she believed herself to be. Marisol speaks with grief about having once been a happy woman and now feeling miserable most of the time. She is not simply sad; she feels altered, as though the version of herself that could laugh easily and trust the goodness of people has receded from reach. Working in ministry has made this especially painful. Her role places her in daily contact with need, dependence, and human vulnerability, and she has come to feel that her old faith in people, in life, and in God has been badly damaged. She still goes through the motions of service, but inwardly she feels estranged from the beliefs that once gave her work meaning.

By the time she sought help, the strain of living this way had become difficult to conceal. She was exhausted by constant tension and by the effort of keeping herself tightly controlled. She was troubled by how quickly her mind moved to danger in silence and delays, and by how little relief she felt even in safe places. What finally brought her in was not one dramatic crisis but the recognition that her world had narrowed around fear, guilt, and shame, and that she could no longer find words for what had happened without feeling overwhelmed. She says she wants some part of her life back, though she is frightened that speaking of the rape will make the images sharper and the guilt worse. What she hopes, quietly and almost cautiously, is that she might someday be able to be still without feeling threatened, and to inhabit her own body without shame.

Juan, a 54-year-old Latin American man, works as a parole officer in a bustling city. His role often puts him on the frontlines of dealing with individuals who have recently been released from incarceration. Despite his dedication to his job, Juan’s life took a significant turn one night when he witnessed an incident of police violence that has left lasting psychological scars. It was a routine call for assistance involving a parolee in distress. When Juan arrived at the scene, he found himself amidst a chaotic confrontation between the parolee and a group of police officers. The situation quickly escalated as the parolee became agitated, and the officers responded with force, leading to his severe injury. Witnessing this event left Juan profoundly shaken. Since that night, Juan has experienced recurrent intrusive thoughts about the incident. He often wakes up in the middle of the night, drenched in sweat, reliving the violent scene. During the day, he finds himself unable to concentrate on work or engage fully with his family. Simple triggers like sirens or uniforms can send him into a state of heightened arousal and anxiety. Juan’s relationship with his wife has also been strained. He becomes irritable easily and often withdraws from her attempts at conversation. His wife feels frustrated by his constant need for solitude, though she knows he is struggling. Recently, Juan has begun to avoid certain areas of the city where similar incidents might occur. This avoidance extends to work-related situations; he now hesitates when called out on emergency calls involving police presence. At work, Juan’s performance has been affected by his inability to focus. His colleagues have noticed a change in him—where once he was reliable and composed, he now seems distant and preoccupied. He often finds himself reenacting the incident mentally during meetings or while writing reports, which hinders his ability to complete tasks efficiently. Juan also engages in hyper-vigilant behaviors that manifest as constant scanning of his surroundings for any potential threats. While walking home from work, he is acutely aware of every sound and movement around him, a state that leaves him feeling perpetually on edge. This heightened state of alertness has made everyday activities exhausting. In addition to these symptoms, Juan experiences intense guilt over the incident. He questions whether there was something more he could have done to prevent it, though logically he knows this wasn’t possible given the circumstances. These thoughts are intrusive and distressing, often surfacing during quiet moments or when he’s alone at home. Juan's marriage has been another area where his PTSD symptoms are evident. His wife, Margarita, feels a growing distance between them as Juan becomes more isolated. She tries to reach out with empathy but struggles to understand the full extent of what her husband is experiencing. Recently, they had a heated argument when she asked him why he couldn't just put the incident behind him, not realizing that it was much more complex for Juan. Despite his efforts to maintain normalcy at work and home, Juan finds himself increasingly overwhelmed by the intrusive memories and emotional distress. He often spends evenings alone in his study, trying to sort through the chaos of his thoughts and emotions. The sense of unease has become a constant companion, making it difficult for him to relax or engage fully with life. Juan’s PTSD symptoms have made daily functioning challenging. Yet, he continues to show up at work each day, driven by his commitment to helping parolees navigate their return to society. Despite the internal turmoil, Juan remains dedicated to his role as a parole officer, though the weight of his experience is palpable in every aspect of his life. Juan’s story underscores the profound impact that witnessing violence can have on an individual's mental health and daily functioning, highlighting the complex interplay between trauma, personal resilience, and the challenges faced by those in high-stress occupations.

Rosa's Silence

Rosa Martínez had been a social ministry worker for twelve years, moving through her parish and the surrounding neighborhoods with a kind of easy competence that made people trust her. She was the sort of woman who knew everyone's name, who brought tamales to the sick, who could sit with a grieving family and say the right thing without seeming to search for it. Her faith had been woven into everything—not performative, but lived. She had believed in redemption, in God's presence in suffering, in the possibility of repair. That was who she had been before the evening in March when a man she knew from the neighborhood followed her into the storage room at the back of the parish hall.

She had been alone there, gathering supplies for the Sunday school. The door had closed behind him. What happened in those minutes had left her with disconnected images rather than a coherent narrative—his hand over her mouth, the cold metal of the shelving unit against her spine, the smell of his sweat and the detergent from the cleaning supplies. Afterward, she had not called the police. She had gone home, showered, and told her husband Miguel that she had felt unwell and gone home early. The man had not been arrested. He still lived in the neighborhood.

In the weeks that followed, Rosa noticed changes in herself that seemed to accumulate like small stones in her chest. She stopped going to the parish hall. Then she stopped attending Mass. The idea of sitting in silence during the liturgy made her skin prickle with dread—silence had become a harbinger, a space where danger pooled. She found herself unable to sit still even at home, unable to sink into the couch or the bed without a sensation of exposure, as though relaxation itself was an invitation to something terrible. She had come to believe that staying vigilant, staying tense, was the only thing protecting her. To let her body go soft felt like offering herself up again.

Her eating had become a rigid architecture. She counted calories obsessively, refused second helpings, sometimes skipped meals altogether. It was the one thing she could control absolutely—what went into her body, how much, when. Everything else had been taken. This, at least, was hers. Miguel had noticed, had asked if she was sick, but she deflected. She could not explain to him that the act of eating, of taking something in, triggered a shame so acute it made her throat close. Her body had become foreign to her, a thing that had been used, that could not be trusted, that she now monitored and restricted as though it were a dangerous animal requiring careful handling.

By autumn, six months after the assault, Rosa's work had begun to suffer. She called in sick more often. When she did go to the ministry office, she found herself unable to focus during the long planning meetings. Any unexpected silence—a pause while someone searched for a word, a moment before a colleague answered—sent her mind spiraling into certainty that something was wrong, that someone was about to tell her bad news, that danger was imminent. She would find her hands shaking. When a home visit took longer than the scheduled hour, she convinced herself that an accident had occurred, that something catastrophic was unfolding. She would cut visits short and return to the office in a state of agitation that she could not fully explain.

What frightened her most was the guilt. When the memories surfaced—and they came as snapshots, fragmented moments that felt more like photographs than film—she was flooded with a conviction that she had somehow caused it, that she had deserved it, that God was punishing her for something. She had lost her faith entirely. The God she had served seemed absent, indifferent, or worse, complicit. The happiness she had carried with her for so long had been replaced by a constant, grinding misery that she could not articulate to anyone. When her supervisor gently asked if everything was all right, Rosa could not find the words. She knew what had happened to her, but something in her mind refused to translate it into language. The silence inside her had become absolute.

It was Miguel who finally insisted she see someone. He had noticed her weight loss, her sleeplessness, the way she flinched at unexpected sounds. He had also noticed that she no longer laughed, that she had withdrawn from their friends, that she had become a different woman—one he loved but no longer recognized. Rosa had resisted. Talking about it felt dangerous, like opening a door that could never be closed. But the weight of carrying it alone had become unbearable, and so she had made an appointment. As she sat in the waiting room, her hands folded tightly in her lap, she was uncertain whether she was hoping to be healed or simply hoping to disappear.

Walter, a 71-year-old man of Oceanic descent, sat quietly in his small living room, the muted colors of the furniture echoing the tranquility he so desperately sought but seldom found. He had been married for nearly 50 years, and though his wife, Lani, was a constant source of support, Walter felt an ever-growing chasm between them, filled with memories he could not articulate. He had been a cashier for most of his life, finding solace in the predictable rhythm of scanning items and making change. But lately, even that had become a challenge, cluttered with memories that intruded at the most unexpected moments.

It had been five years since he witnessed the horrific accident outside the grocery store where he worked. A frantic mother had lost control of her car, careening onto the sidewalk where children played. Walter had been on break that day, stepping outside for a breath of fresh air. The sound of the impact was deafening, followed by the piercing cries of a baby. The scene unfolded in front of him like a nightmare, with chaos erupting and people rushing to help, but all he could focus on were the cries of that innocent child. The wailing seemed to echo in his mind, and even now, the sound of a baby crying could send him spiraling back to that moment, heart racing and breath quickening, as if the threat were still present.

Since then, Walter's life had become a series of carefully constructed barriers against the world. He avoided the grocery store’s entrance whenever possible, opting instead for the back door, fearing the sound of doors opening or slamming would trigger the visceral memories he tried so hard to suppress. On days when Lani encouraged him to join her on errands, he would tense up at the slightest unexpected movement nearby, reacting as if danger loomed, as if the shadows of that day were stalking him still. He had come to believe that if he kept a watchful eye on everyone around him, he could somehow protect himself from reliving that horror. It was a reluctant habit, one that made him feel like a prisoner in his own mind, but it felt necessary—he had to stay vigilant.

The memories from that day were an incomplete picture, fragments that haunted him without a clear narrative to anchor them. He would sit in silence, trying to piece together what had happened, but it was as if the threads of the story slipped through his fingers like sand. When Lani would ask him to recount the events, he would struggle to find the words, often losing the thread midway through, leaving both of them frustrated and confused. Walter had begun to feel dead inside, emotionally numb. He could not shake the feeling that the institutions meant to protect him—his workplace, the police, the emergency responders—had all failed. No one had been held accountable, and that gnawed at him like an open wound.

In the months that followed the accident, Walter's avoidance grew more pronounced. He stopped attending family gatherings and avoided places where children might be present. Lani noticed his increasing discomfort and tried to coax him out of the house, but he would often decline, preferring the safety of their home. The once jovial conversations turned into strained silence, and though he loved Lani deeply, he felt he was becoming a shell of the man she had married.

It was only recently, during a quiet evening after a particularly triggering day at work, that Walter finally recognized the breadth of his suffering. An unexpected slam of the door had sent him spiraling into panic, and he found himself crying in the bathroom, the sound of his own muffled sobs reminding him of that child’s cries. It was in that moment that he understood he could no longer navigate this alone. The weight of his experiences, the fear that clung to him like a second skin, had reached a tipping point. 

Now, as he sat in the therapist's office, Walter felt a mixture of fear and hope. He was afraid of having to relive the trauma, of confronting the emotions he had buried for so long. But he also held onto a flicker of hope that perhaps, through this process, he could reclaim the pieces of himself that had been lost. He wanted to tell his story, to make sense of the chaos, and to find a way back to the man he once was—a man who could enjoy the laughter of children without feeling the sting of past pain.

Carlos was a 65-year-old dentist when a lone gunman opened fire on a crowded cultural fair in his city. He had been walking with his wife, who was killed beside him. He survived physically, but the memory of that afternoon never settled—it returned as a complete sensory reliving, overwhelming him with the same sounds, smells, and terror every time. He could not put it into words; the experience was too raw, too wordless, too much to hold in language.

In the months after, he began to notice changes. A car backfiring on the street would stop him cold—the gunshot noise alone could send him into a full recall of the attack, his heart racing, the scene flooding back as if he were still there. He became hyperalert to unexpected sounds and started watching other people closely for signs that they might harm him. Whenever he entered a room or building, he automatically scanned for exits. At work in his dental practice, a patient’s mention of military service or a uniformed officer stopping for a routine check made his chest tighten—authority figures in uniform were now potent triggers.

He came to believe he had failed at the fair, that he should have seen it coming or shielded his wife. This self-blame became a recurring rumination, each cycle of guilt pulling him back into the memory of the event, the sights and sounds returning with fresh intensity. To feel safer, he began carrying a concealed handgun. The weight of the weapon in his jacket pocket was a constant reminder of vulnerability—it also made him more sensitive to any sound that could be a gunshot, and he found himself avoiding news reports about similar attacks because they brought the memory roaring back.

His hypervigilance to threatening sounds kept him on edge, which reinforced his urge to carry the weapon and to avoid military topics or news. The avoidance, in turn, removed any chance to habituate to the triggers, so a single unexpected noise remained capable of triggering a full sensory flashback. And the flashbacks, overwhelming as they were, made him even more watchful of others and more likely to scan exits before he could settle. His rumination about blame made the memory more vivid, and the vivid memory made him more sensitive to any potential trigger—a cycle he could not break.

Carlos retired from dentistry last year, partly because the clinical environment—the drills, the sudden sounds, the anxious patients—had become a landscape of triggers. He still carries the handgun everywhere, and his children have expressed concern. He rarely visits them because their neighborhood is near a military base, and conversations about deployment are too jarring. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at a grocery store: a uniformed security guard startled him, his hand went to his pocket, and he realized he had reached for his gun in public. He is afraid of what he might do, and more afraid of what he might feel if he lets the memory surface without his avoidance.

Maria is a 57-year-old woman who owns a small grocery store in a bustling community. Her days are often filled with the familiar sounds of the cash register dinging, customers chatting, and the faint hum of the refrigerator in the back. However, beneath the surface of her daily routine lies a current of anxiety that has become increasingly difficult for her to ignore.

The trauma began three years ago when her youngest child, Amina, was diagnosed with a rare and life-threatening illness. Maria remembers that day with a clarity that feels like a raw wound. They had gone to the hospital for what she thought was a routine check-up. Amina, then just twelve, was cheerful and chatty, oblivious to the storm that would soon engulf their family. As the doctor delivered the news, Maria’s world shattered. The room spun, and the doctor’s voice faded into a muffled echo, leaving her with a suffocating sense of dread.

In the months that followed, Maria plunged into a relentless cycle of worry and despair. Each hospital visit was a gauntlet of fear; the antiseptic smell of the hospital, the sterile white walls, and the sound of machines beeping became triggers that sent her spiraling. She recalls how she would stand beside Amina's bed, her heart racing, feeling as if she might collapse under the weight of her helplessness. Watching her daughter fight for her life was a torment that gnawed at Maria’s soul, and she often felt as if she were drowning in a sea of anxiety. 

During this time, Maria struggled to maintain her grocery store. Once a source of pride and joy, it became a mere obligation. The vibrant chatter of customers, which she once cherished, now felt like an overwhelming cacophony, reminding her of the life she was desperately trying to hold together. She often found herself zoning out mid-conversation, her thoughts drifting back to Amina’s hospital room, to the beeping machines, and to the doctors’ grave faces. 

As Amina’s health fluctuated, so did Maria’s mental state. Amina would have moments of improvement, but they always felt shadowed by the looming fear of a relapse. Maria began experiencing sleepless nights filled with nightmares that replayed her daughter’s suffering, waking up in a cold sweat, her heart pounding as she struggled to differentiate between sleep and reality. During the day, she would sometimes find herself frozen in place, her mind racing with thoughts of “What if?” and “I can’t lose her.” 

Her husband, Raj, tried to be supportive, but Maria often felt isolated. She would brush off his attempts to talk, fearing that expressing her feelings would only deepen her pain. Instead, she buried herself in her work, keeping longer hours at the store to distract herself from her spiraling emotions. However, the longer she worked, the more exhausted she became, and the less capable she felt of coping with the realities of her life.

Now, three years later, Amina is stable but still requires ongoing care. Maria’s trauma has not faded; instead, it has woven itself into the fabric of her being. She often finds herself replaying the hospital scenes in her mind, and the sudden sounds of laughter in the store can trigger a wave of anxiety, transporting her back to those harrowing days. 

Her friends coax her into small gatherings, but she struggles to engage. The laughter and joy of others feel like a foreign language; she feels detached, as if she is merely observing life from a distance. At home, when Amina is at school, Maria sometimes sits in silence, staring at the walls, feeling like a ghost in her own life.

As she continues to navigate her days, the grocery store remains a refuge and a reminder of her resilience. It is filled with familiar faces and the mundane rhythm of life that she clings to, even as she grapples with her own tumultuous emotions. Maria recognizes that she is not the same person she once was, but she holds onto the hope that she can eventually find her way back to herself, one day at a time.

Rafael Moreno is a 70-year-old widowed dentist who came to treatment after years of trying to manage on his own what happened during a terrorist attack. He describes the event haltingly and only in fragments, because when he gets close to it he becomes so flooded that he has to stop speaking. Even in early sessions, he would begin, press his lips together, and lift a hand as if to hold the memory back. He said more than once that he could not really put it into words. What returns to him is not a story with a beginning and end so much as a total sensory experience that feels as if it is happening again: the crack of gunfire, the confusion in the room, the presence of armed men, the bodily certainty that death was near. The most he has been able to convey consistently is that he was in a public place when the attack began, that there were men in uniform amid the chaos, and that the sound of gunshots is what still reaches him first, before any thought does.

In the months after the attack, Rafael did what he had always done in his professional life: he tried to stay controlled, practical, and prepared. He returned to his dental practice, but his days began to narrow around signs of danger. The first thing he noticed on entering any building, including his own office, was where the exits were. He would register them before he noticed the receptionist’s greeting or the patient schedule. In the waiting room he found himself studying people closely, not out of curiosity but from a felt need to judge whether anyone might be dangerous. A patient shifting suddenly in his seat, a stranger lingering near the front desk, a delivery worker in a uniform stepping into the suite could change the whole atmosphere for him in an instant. He would feel his body tighten before he had fully taken in why.

Specific things came to carry a charge that was immediately understandable to him, even if he hated living this way. People in uniform were especially difficult. A police officer walking past the storefront below his office, a security guard in a medical building, even seeing someone dressed in a style that reminded him of military clothing would pull his attention hard. Conversations about the military were almost as bad. If patients or colleagues began talking about deployments, weapons, wars, or “service,” Rafael felt himself leaving the present and bracing internally, as though something threatening were already unfolding around him. Gunshot noises were the most potent of all. Fireworks, a car backfiring, a sharp bang from construction near the office could send him into immediate alarm. He described being on high alert with any loud or unexpected sound, his body reacting before his mind caught up.

Over time, Rafael built his life around reducing contact with anything that might bring the attack too close. He stopped watching news coverage about shootings, bombings, or attacks because even a brief report could leave him shaken for hours. He began carrying a weapon, telling himself that at his age, living alone after his wife’s death, it was only sensible to be able to protect himself. He knew this was not how he had lived before, but the weapon gave him a sense that he was not entirely exposed. Alongside this, another pattern settled in: he repeatedly blamed himself for what had happened. He would replay scraps of the day and circle around the same questions—whether he should have noticed something earlier, moved faster, chosen a different place to stand, done more for other people. These thoughts did not resolve into answers, but he returned to them again and again.

The strain has become visible in the texture of his daily life. At the practice, he schedules fewer patients and dislikes being in the office when there is unfamiliar foot traffic in the hallway. He has become more guarded with staff and more distracted when sudden noises break the routine of the day. Socially he is narrower too, avoiding situations where current events are likely to come up. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident at work when a sharp bang from nearby construction made the memory return with such force that he had to stop in the middle of the day and shut himself in his office. He said it was as if the attack had arrived whole, through sound and sensation, and for several minutes he was no longer certain he was in his dental practice. That frightened him not only because of how real it felt, but because he could see how much of his life had come to revolve around staying ready, staying armed, staying watchful. What he hopes for now is modest but deeply felt: to be able to walk into his own office without first planning escape, to hear a loud sound without feeling that he is back there, and to speak about what happened without being overtaken by it.

He was twenty-one when the water came, and now, at twenty-two, he still smells it in his dreams. Not the rain—that he could handle—but the thick, brown smell of the river rising through his apartment in Bangkok. He remembers the sound first: a low hum that became a growl, then a crash as the wall gave way. He grabbed his laptop, his phone, his grandmother’s photograph, and climbed to the roof with three neighbors. They stayed there for fourteen hours while the water swallowed the ground floor, swallowing the motorbikes, the street vendors, the family photographs he’d left behind.

Now he works as a UX designer for a midsize tech firm in a glass building that looks nothing like his old neighborhood. He lives in a new high-rise on the tenth floor, far from the river. But every morning, when the elevator doors close, his chest tightens. He takes the stairs now, all ten flights, because the elevator feels like the roof of that building—a small, wet space with no way out. His colleagues don’t notice. They see a quiet, meticulous young man who arranges his desk in perfect order, who checks the weather app obsessively, who never takes the elevator.

At work, he designs interfaces for a ride-hailing app. Last month, his manager asked him to create a flood-alert feature for the app’s safety dashboard. He nodded, opened a new file, and sat staring at the blank screen for three hours. The cursor blinked like a heartbeat. When he finally closed the file, his hands were shaking. He told his manager the feature needed more user research. He is still avoiding it.

The sounds are the worst. A loud bang from a delivery truck backfiring sends him under his desk before he can stop himself. He stays there, knees to chest, counting the seconds until his heart slows. His coworkers have started to notice. One of them, a kind woman named Priya, asked if he was okay. He said he was fine, just tired. He has said “just tired” so many times that he believes it might be true. But tired people don’t wake up at 3 a.m. gasping for air, convinced the bed is floating. Tired people don’t check the weather forecast six times before leaving the apartment.

He hasn’t been to a movie theater since the flood. The darkness, the loud sound, the way the screen fills your whole vision—it feels too much like being trapped on that roof, watching the water rise. He used to love action films. Now he watches only quiet shows on his laptop, in a well-lit room, with the door open.

He hasn’t called his mother in three weeks. She lives in the same city, in a different flood zone. He knows she is fine—she texts him every day—but hearing her voice makes him see that water again, the way it floated her kitchen table out the door. He will call tomorrow. He said that yesterday, too.

On good days, he can focus on wireframes and user flows. He is good at his job. He understands how people move through digital spaces, what frustrates them, what soothes them. But lately, he has been sketching the same thing over and over in the margins of his notebook: a small house on a hill, surrounded by a blue line that never quite reaches the door. He doesn’t know what it means, or why he can’t stop drawing it.

He is twenty-two. The flood was a year ago. He still checks the door is unlocked, then locked, then unlocked again. He still sleeps with the lights on. He still finds himself holding his breath whenever the clouds turn gray. He is tired of being tired. But he doesn’t know how to stop running from the water that is no longer there.

Three years ago, she was a logistics officer in a war zone, moving supplies through a corridor known for ambushes. That day, the convoy stopped for a disabled vehicle. She stepped out to assess the damage, clipboard in hand, when the first mortar hit. The blast threw her against a shipping container. She remembers the ringing in her ears, the taste of dust and copper, the burning fuel smell, and the voice of a dying driver calling for his mother. She does not remember pulling him from the wreckage, but photographs later showed her there, hands covered in blood.

Now she sits in a sterile cubicle, the faint hum of fluorescent lights replacing the whine of mortars. She is an auditor for a state agency. Her desk is arranged with geometric precision: pens aligned, papers squared, a single coaster for her coffee. She checks each column of numbers three times, sometimes four, because one wrong digit could mean a million-dollar error—and in her mind, errors are not mistakes, they are failures that cost lives. Her supervisor praises her thoroughness, but she knows it is not thoroughness. It is fear.

The divorce is two years old. He was a civilian, a man who loved her calm, analytical mind. After her deployment ended, she could not sleep beside him. She would wake on the living room floor, knife in hand, certain someone was in the apartment. He stopped touching her without warning because she would flinch, sometimes swing. He told her last argument that she was not living with him, she was living inside a war. She agreed. She signed the papers without looking back.

At work, she avoids the break room after 12:30 p.m. because that is when the trash truck reverses outside, making the same beep-beep-beep as the armored vehicle that exploded in the ambush. She has not used the company elevator since the time it stopped between floors for twenty seconds; she clawed at the doors, hyperventilating, and now she takes the stairs five flights up, even with a bad knee. People think she is health-conscious. She does not correct them.

Her mind feels fractured. She has no memory of whole weeks during the early years back home. Now she remembers too much: the metallic click of a rifle bolt, the smell of diesel and sweat, the exact shade of red the sky turned before the second mortar hit. She sees these images while sitting at her desk, while driving, while listening to a colleague talk about weekend plans. She cannot stop them.

She stopped going to her daughter's soccer games because the crowd noise—the cheers, the whistles—sounds like the panic of a stampede. Instead, she watches video recordings at 2 a.m., alone, volume muted. She has not hugged her daughter in over a year. She does not know how to explain.

Some nights she walks through her apartment, checking locks repeatedly, as if she were still responsible for guarding a perimeter. She keeps a suitcase packed under her bed with essentials—change of clothes, cash, water purification tablets. She tells herself it is practical. She does not tell herself that it is the same bag she carried through the war.

Her therapist has asked her to describe what the world feels like now. She says it is like wearing scratched goggles. Everything is there, but nothing is quite clear. She is waiting for the next mortar to fall, even though she knows there are no mortars here. The waiting never stops.

Ernesto Villanueva is a 70-year-old widowed dentist of Colombian origin who has practiced in the same Miami clinic for nearly three decades. He came to the United States as a young man, built a quiet, ordered life, and prided himself on a steadiness that his patients and colleagues had always remarked upon. That steadiness was fractured approximately fourteen months ago when Ernesto was present at a civic ceremony in a public park — a local festival he attended every year — when a politically motivated attack unfolded without warning. Armed men in paramilitary-style clothing moved through the crowd, firing weapons and shouting directives. Ernesto was pinned behind a vendor's cart for what felt to him like an eternity, pressed against the ground, listening to shots ring out at irregular intervals, watching uniformed figures move past him with weapons raised. He was not physically wounded, but a man standing near him was struck and fell. Ernesto did not run. He stayed still, and he has never fully made peace with that fact.

In the weeks after the attack, Ernesto returned to his practice because he did not know what else to do. The clinic's routine — the hum of the suction unit, the bright overhead lights, the predictable sequencing of appointments — offered something that resembled normalcy. But the world outside the operatory had become a different place. When a car backfired on the street near his clinic, Ernesto found himself gripping the edge of the sink, unable to move for several seconds, the park flooding back through him not as a recollection but as a full sensory return: the smell of the grass, the weight of the ground beneath him, the sound of the shots as immediate and present as if they were occurring in the room. When the memory came in those moments, it did not arrive as narrative — he could not have told anyone, in ordered sentences, what had happened or in what sequence. It came as sensation, as texture, as the particular quality of light that afternoon, and it overwhelmed him so completely that he sometimes had to excuse himself from a patient mid-procedure and stand in the back hallway until the wave passed.

Ernesto had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable to him, that he should have done something more — pulled the man beside him to safety, acted rather than frozen. He returned to this conclusion repeatedly, rehearsing the moment from every angle, always arriving at the same verdict against himself. He began avoiding the evening news, because any report touching on political violence or armed groups confirmed, in his mind, that the world remained exactly as dangerous as it had been that afternoon. He started carrying a licensed firearm, which he kept in his car and sometimes in the inner pocket of his jacket, because what frightened him most was the idea of being caught without any means of response again.

At the clinic, the consequences of these changes became visible in ways Ernesto could not fully conceal. When a patient arrived wearing a security guard's uniform for an afternoon appointment, Ernesto felt his chest tighten and his attention fracture entirely. He got through the appointment by watching the man's hands. He now scans the waiting room each morning before unlocking the front door — not consciously cataloguing exits, but moving his eyes to every corner and doorway in a sweep that has become as automatic as washing his hands. He monitors his patients and his staff with a vigilance that has no clinical purpose, reading faces for signs of something he cannot name precisely but recognises immediately as threat.

A colleague gently noted that Ernesto seemed changed, and that several patients had mentioned he seemed distracted. A conversation about a recent news story involving military operations in South America left Ernesto unable to concentrate for the remainder of the afternoon. It was his daughter, calling from Bogotá, who finally said what had been unsaid — that her father did not sound like himself, and had not for over a year. Ernesto made the appointment the following week. What he most hopes for is to be able to remember what happened without being destroyed by it each time. What he fears most is that the man he was before the park no longer exists.

Dr. Ernesto Moralez is a seventy-year-old man who retired from dentistry five years ago, though his hands still remember the precise angle of a mirror and the weight of a handpiece. In his two-bedroom house in a quiet Miami suburb, he keeps his old dental license framed in the study, next to a faded photograph of his wife, Marta, who died of cancer six years ago. He rarely looks at either.

The story Ernesto tells begins on a Tuesday morning in Lima, thirty-seven years ago. He was forty-three, married, the father of two young daughters, and the owner of a well-regarded dental practice near the Plaza San Martín. That morning he had a full schedule: a root canal, a set of impressions, a child with a cavity. At 10:15, a bomb concealed in a delivery van detonated across the street, directly outside a government building. The blast wave shattered his office windows, sent glass and debris through the treatment room. Ernesto was bent over a patient, mid-procedure, when the pressure threw him against the cabinet. He remembers the ringing, the dust, the patient’s scream, the blood from a shard embedded in his own forearm.

Three people died in the street. Six more were injured, including the patient in his chair—a young mother, who lost an eye from flying glass. Ernesto stopped working that day. He cleaned the wounds of his staff, then walked home in a daze and told Marta he could not go back. He sold the practice within a month, and the family immigrated to the United States.

Now, in the present, Ernesto lives a quiet life. He does not go to public plazas. He avoids crowded places, especially streets with parked delivery vans. When he sees a commercial truck idling near a building, his chest tightens, his palms sweat, and he crosses to the other side without thinking. To himself, he calls this “just being careful,” but he knows it is more. He has not visited a city center in years. He stopped driving after a flashback at a red light—the honking, the sunlight flickering through windshield glass, the sudden memory of the blast’s white light—and now his daughter drives him to appointments.

At home, he mostly watches television with the volume low. He sleeps in the living room recliner, because the bedroom reminds him of Marta and because lying flat leaves him vulnerable to intrusive images: the woman’s face, the slice of glass, the ringing that never quite stopped. He wakes often, startled by the sound of a motorcycle backfire or a garbage truck’s hydraulic hiss. Once, he dropped a glass of water in the kitchen and the shattering sent him to the floor, hands over his head, breathing fast.

His daughters, now grown, think he is simply aging. He does not correct them. He visits their homes but never stays long, and he refuses invitations to grandchildren’s birthday parties at indoor play spaces or restaurants. “I prefer here,” he says, gesturing at his own small back patio.

He still uses his dental skills in small ways—polishing a chipped molar with a file he keeps in a drawer, examining his own teeth in the bathroom mirror each morning with the same methodical eye. But when his granddaughter had a toothache last spring, he recommended a dentist he knew, and he could not bring himself to explain why he could not treat her himself: the smell of eugenol, the sound of suction, the memory of that Tuesday curling around him like smoke.

He does not speak of the bombing. He tells himself it was long ago. But the present is narrow: a house, a television, a daughter’s phone call, a careful path to the grocery store before noon, avoiding the main street. At night, alone, he sometimes hears the explosion again, as clear as a cracked bell, and he waits for dawn with his hand on the arm of the recliner, heart hammering, a retired dentist holding still.

Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was thirty-four when he came to his first appointment, referred by his primary care physician after his wife, Elena, had finally insisted he see someone. He sat with his shoulders pressed against the back of the chair, positioned so that he could see the door of the consulting room without turning his head. He had noticed the exit the moment he walked in—a habit so automatic now that he could not remember when it had started, though he knew exactly when it had become necessary.

Six years earlier, Marcus had taken a leave of absence from the fire department to work as a relief worker in a conflict zone in the Levant. He had been there for four months, helping to coordinate medical supplies and assist with evacuations in a region where the distinction between civilian and combatant had become meaningless. On his forty-third day, the compound where he and twelve others were sheltering came under sustained fire. He had been in the courtyard when the first rounds hit. He remembered the sound—not loud but precise, almost clinical—and then the chaos of bodies moving without coordination, people calling out names that went unanswered. A colleague beside him fell. Marcus dragged him toward what he thought was cover, but the angle was wrong; there was no real shelter. He spent eighteen minutes in that courtyard, certain that each second would be his last, listening to rounds strike concrete and flesh with equal indifference.

He was not physically injured. When the firing stopped, he helped carry the wounded to a vehicle. He finished his rotation. He came home.

For the first year back, Marcus told Elena that he was fine, just tired. He returned to the fire department. But something had shifted in how he understood space and safety. He had come to believe that threats could materialize anywhere, that ordinary environments contained hidden dangers, that strangers—people he passed on the street, customers at the grocery store, even the new neighbor who had knocked on his door to introduce himself—might pose a risk he could not anticipate or control. His mind had developed a kind of scanning protocol: entering any room, he would immediately locate the exits, assess sightlines, note potential obstacles. In the firehouse, this felt almost professional; in his own living room, it felt like a betrayal of the life he was supposed to be living.

Within months, Marcus had stopped going to the gym. He had always lifted weights three times a week, a ritual that steadied him. But gyms were enclosed spaces with limited exits, full of strangers, and the vulnerability of exertion felt intolerable. He told Elena it was just a scheduling issue. Then he stopped going out for evening walks through their neighborhood. The open streets felt worse in some ways—too many people, too many angles of approach. At home, he positioned himself always with a view of the door. He began to tense when Elena tried to hold him, when she wanted to celebrate small things—a promotion at her law firm, their anniversary—because joy felt dangerous, a kind of exposure. When she reached for him with genuine happiness in her face, something in him recoiled. He had come to believe that positive feelings made you careless, that they softened your vigilance, that they were a luxury he could not afford.

Elena had watched him disappear into hypervigilance over five years. She saw how his shoulders never fully relaxed, how he would sometimes grip her arm too tightly when a car backfired, how he had become a ghost in their marriage—present but sealed off, always listening for a threat that never came. When she tried to talk to him about it, he would acknowledge that yes, he knew it was irrational, but knowing and feeling were different things. The rational part of him understood that their quiet suburban street was safe. The part of him that had spent eighteen minutes in that courtyard knew better.

Marcus came to therapy because Elena had given him an ultimatum, but also because he was exhausted. He was afraid of what his hypervigilance might cost him—his marriage, his career, his mind. He was hoping that someone could help him understand why safety, even when objectively present, still felt like a luxury he had forfeited.
